Why this exists

I came to medicine from the outside. I studied business and data science, worked in healthcare consulting, and only later found my way to medical school, so I remember exactly what medical evidence looks like to everyone else: locked behind jargon, paywalls, and papers written for other researchers. The science was sound. The communication was not, and people were left making real decisions about their own bodies from whatever fragments they could piece together. My mind has always worked the other way: take something complicated and make it digestible without making it smaller. So I built The PM&R Files, visual essays that treat readers as smart, show the actual numbers behind rehabilitation medicine, say plainly what the evidence cannot prove, and open a field that too often talks only to itself.

Jonathan Byrne, DO · Founder

The PM&R Files · Essay 17

Every Prescription Is a Bet

Medicine runs on odds. This essay reads one prescription the way an actuary would: as a priced bet on a single life.

Jonathan Byrne, DO · PM&R residentDRAFT: pending expert review

Start with one small white pill: aspirin. In a large trial of people with diabetes, aspirin stopped one heart attack or stroke for every 91 people who took it. In that same trial, it caused one major bleed for every 111. Help and harm, side by side, at nearly the same size.

That is not a fact about aspirin. It is the shape of almost every choice in medicine. Each drug, each test, each operation is a bet: some chance of gain, some chance of loss, and one person who has to live with how it lands.

So here is the claim of this essay. Good medicine is good betting. Not gambling, which is betting blind. Betting with the odds worked out, the stakes priced, and the size of the bet matched to the person in front of you. The field that does this for a living is not medicine. It is actuarial science, the math of pricing risk. Medicine borrowed its tools long ago. It just rarely says so.

Bet slip No. 17The five fields on every slip

The event
One bad thing, or not, in a set span of time
The odds
How often it strikes people like this patient
The edge
How much the treatment cuts those odds
The price
What the treatment costs in harm
The payout
The number needed to treat

A note from the person who wrote this slip. Before medical school, I interned in actuarial consulting and worked as a health care analytics analyst. I priced risk for groups of strangers. Now I treat one person at a time, and the same math keeps showing up at the bedside.

Scroll · the slip fills in

Slip section 01 · The machinery

First, the odds had to be invented

The tools on this slip feel like medicine. They are not. They were built to price lives for money, and the dates give it away.

1693

A price list for lives

Edmond Halley, an astronomer, took the birth and death records of one city, Breslau, and built a table: how many people are still alive at each age. The title of his paper says what it was for. It ends with the words “an attempt to ascertain the price of annuities upon lives.” The first life table was a pricing tool.

1825

Risk compounds like interest

Benjamin Gompertz, who worked in insurance, found the law inside the table. The risk of death does not grow in a straight line as we age. It compounds, at a steady rate, the way interest does. He wrote the math down to value life contracts: what a promise to pay is worth when no one knows how long a life will run.

1958

The table learns to lose people

Two statisticians, Edward Kaplan and Paul Meier, fixed the table's weak point. Real patients move away, quit, and get lost. Their method still counts each person fairly up to the day they vanish. It is called the Kaplan-Meier curve, and almost every survival curve in every drug trial since is this table's grandchild.

Hold on to one point. None of this was built to heal. It was built to price. Medicine took the tools over because the tools work. This essay borrows them back for a few pages.

Slip section 02 · The odds machine

Place the bet

Meet the patient on this slip. She has atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that lets blood pool in the heart, where it can clot. A clot that breaks loose can cause a stroke. A blood thinner cuts that risk a lot. It also makes bleeding more likely. So: bet, or no bet?

The price of the bet hangs on one score. The CHA2DS2-VASc score gives points for heart failure, high blood pressure, diabetes, blood vessel disease, age, and sex, with two points each for age 75 or older and for a past stroke or clot. More points, more risk. Tap a score. The slip reprices at once.

Your patient's score
71 patient-years of blood thinner to prevent one stroke Good bet
Stroke risk, no treatment2.2% a year
Strokes prevented14.1 per 1,000per year of treatment
Major bleeds added, the harm lineUnder 3 per 1,000per year, at every score
Prevented
Bleeds

Plainly: of 1,000 people with a score of 2, treated for one year, the drug prevents about 14 strokes.

The math on this slip: benefit = baseline risk × 64%. Warfarin, the blood thinner in the trials, cut stroke risk by 64% (Hart 2007). The baselines come from 182,678 people with this condition in Sweden (Friberg 2012).

Guidelines draw their line at a score of 2 and up. Watch the verdict flip in the same place the guideline does.

Slip section 03 · Two more slips

The drug never changes. The odds do.

Slip twoA statin, priced over ten years

A statin lowers LDL cholesterol. For each 1 mmol/L drop, the pooled trials find about 21% fewer major vascular events: heart attacks, strokes, and deaths from them (CTT 2005; 90,056 people in 14 trials). Now hold the drug still and move the person.

  • 10 year risk 2.5%NNT 191
  • 10 year risk 5%NNT 95
  • 10 year risk 7.5%NNT 64The line the US guideline draws
  • 10 year risk 10%NNT 48
  • 10 year risk 20%NNT 24
  • 10 year risk 30%NNT 16

Same pill. Same 21%. The only thing that moved was who sat in the chair.

The harm column is real, and its clock runs at a different speed. Treat 255 people for 4 years and about one extra case of diabetes shows up (Sattar 2010). The benefit above is priced over 10 years, the harm over 4. A fair slip shows both clocks.

Slip threeAspirin, the bet that cancels itself

Aspirin went to three big trials in 2018, in three kinds of people. Same drug each time. Three answers.

  • ASCEND15,480 people with diabetes, followed 7.4 years. Prevented: one event per 91 treated. Caused: one major bleed per 111. The trial's own verdict: the gains were largely wiped out by the bleeding.
  • ASPREE19,114 healthy older adults, median age 74. Prevented: nothing that could be measured. Caused: one extra major bleed per 100 treated.
  • ARRIVE12,546 adults at moderate risk. Prevented: nothing clear. Caused: one extra gut bleed per 196 treated.

Three tables, one drug. The people, and their starting odds, did all the talking.

Slip section 04 · The house rules

Every house posts its limits

Casinos post their limits. Medicine posts its own, in guidelines, and they do the same job: they say where a bet turns worth placing, for the average person at the table.

  • 1975Medicine wrote the rule down early. Stephen Pauker and Jerome Kassirer showed that each treatment has a break-even point: a chance of disease above which treating wins, and below which it loses. The point is set by the ratio of harm to benefit. Every rule below is that one idea, dressed for a clinic.
  • 2The stroke slip gets its line at a score of 2. You watched the verdict flip there a screen ago.
  • 7.5%The US cholesterol guideline sets its line at a 10 year risk of 7.5%. Above it, a statin is judged worth it for the average patient. Below it, not.
  • 3% · 20%Bone care runs the same play. Treat when the 10 year chance of a hip fracture hits 3%, or of a major fracture 20%. That is the FRAX score, as used in US practice.
  • £Then the house prices the payout itself. One QALY is one year lived in full health. For years, NICE in England called a treatment good value at £20,000 to £30,000 per QALY. In April 2026, that line rose to £25,000 to £35,000. In the US, the review group ICER uses $100,000 to $150,000 per QALY as its yardstick. Figures checked October 2026.

None of these lines is a law of nature. A committee set each one, the way an underwriter sets the top price for a class of risk. Knowing the line is posted is the first step. Knowing when your patient should cross it is the craft.

Slip section 05 · The fine print

Read the fine print. It is the honest part.

Every real slip has fine print, and most people skip it. Do not. It is set in full size here, on purpose.

Prices vary by book

Across 17 studies of people with atrial fibrillation, the yearly stroke rate at a score of 0 ran from 0 to 2.41 percent. At a score of 2, it ran from about 0.48 to 7.84 percent. The odds on this slip come from one large Swedish group. Your patient may belong to a pricier book, or a cheaper one.

No one is an average

Every risk number is a price quoted for a class of people. You belong to many classes at once: your age group, your sex, people with your blood pressure, people who run marathons. Each class quotes a different price, and no rule can say which class was the right one. The philosopher Hans Reichenbach named this in 1949: the problem of the reference class. A score does not solve it. It picks a class in an orderly way. And the narrower the class, the thinner the data under its price.

Prices can be wrong

When two researchers tested the pooled cohort equations, the formulas US doctors use to price heart risk, on three large groups, the formulas overshot real risk by 75 to 150 percent. A wrong starting price flows through clean math and comes out as a wrong bet, with each step looking exact.

The score is a blunt tool

The stroke score sorts people only fairly well. Its accuracy score, called the c statistic, is about 0.61, where 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect. It still earns its place: a blunt price, stated out loud, beats a guess.

The big number hides its clock

The number needed to treat hides its time frame and its doubt. An event stopped in year one and an event pushed to year nine count the same inside a fixed window. And when a trial's benefit could be zero, as in the ARRIVE aspirin trial, the number runs off through infinity. A neat figure printed there is not a small benefit. It is no measured benefit at all.

The 64% is an assumption

This slip treats warfarin's 64% cut as the same at every score. The large reviews behind it found the cut roughly steady across groups. Roughly steady is an assumption, not a law, and the whole slip leans on it.

Newer drugs, modeled odds

Newer blood thinners beat warfarin by a further 19% in relative terms (Ruff 2014). No trial has tested them against no treatment at all. So any figure for them against nothing is built by chaining two reviews together. This slip prices warfarin only, because warfarin was tested against nothing.

You have to live to collect

A ten year bet assumes the person lives ten years to collect it. Other risks compete, and with age they compound. Gompertz again. Most bedside numbers leave this out. The bone score, FRAX, is one of the few that builds it in.

The last line is yours

The last line of the slip is not about risk. It is about value. The math treats each outcome as the same coin. Patients do not. When researchers asked people living with spinal cord injury what they would want back first, their order was not the one their doctors guessed. That story is Essay 15, What Would You Want Back? The actuary can price the risk. Only the patient can price the outcome. A good slip carries both prices.

The patient's price: ____________________

Nothing here is advice for any one person. These numbers describe groups of people in published studies. A bet this size belongs to a patient and a clinician, with the slip on the table between them.

How the odds machine works: for the score you pick, it takes the Swedish rate of strokes per year with no treatment (Friberg 2012), cuts it by warfarin's 64% (Hart 2007), and turns the gap into a number needed to treat. Patient-years is the total time across people: an NNT of 71 means treating 71 people for one year each prevents about one stroke. Bleeding figures are major bleeds outside the skull, the harm Hart measured. Statin figures apply the CTT's 21% cut to 10 year risks, the frame the US guideline uses. The statin benefit is priced over 10 years and its diabetes harm over 4; both clocks are printed where the numbers appear.

If you had no back pain, what would your MRI say?

By Jonathan Byrne, DO · October 2026

Why this essay: Back pain is the most common thing I see, and the scariest thing patients hear is a radiology report.

A scan can describe the spine in remarkable detail. It cannot, by itself, tell you why a person hurts.

The back pain imaging paradox

Drag your age through eight findings measured in pain-free people, decode the words, and see when imaging changes the question.

SCROLL INTO THE DATA ↓

The older the pain-free spine, the more “abnormal” its MRI looks.

96%of pain-free 80-year-olds were modeled to show disk degeneration.
01 · Your scan02 · The curve03 · The words04 · Counterweight05 · Red flags06 · Reporting07 · Sources
Your scan

Say we scanned you today, with zero back pain. Here's what your MRI would probably say.

These aren't your personal odds. They're group averages: the share of pain-free people at each age who show each finding, modeled from 33 studies1.

Read the denominatorEvery percentage on this page means “among pain-free people of this age.” It is not an individual prediction.
Age-adjusted prevalence · scroll or drag

Among pain-free people your age

Drag the slider to your age. Every bar is the share of pain-free people your age who show that finding.

2080

35 YEARS
ASYMPTOMATIC COHORT
SCROLL-SYNCED VIEW
AGE 20marks accumulate by decade

Model predictions from Brinjikji et al. 2015, AJNR. Values between decades are linearly interpolated by us. Hatched bars at ages 20 to 30: low data. Facet degeneration and spondylolisthesis are model extrapolations from zero direct observations in those age groups.

AGE 20

The first frame

Disk degeneration 37% · bulge 30% · protrusion 29% · annular fissure 19%. Even at 20, pain-free people already carry these words on their scans.

AGE 30

The vocabulary grows

Disk degeneration 52% · bulge 40% · protrusion 31% · annular fissure 20%. The words pile up a decade before most backs ever hurt.

AGE 40

“Abnormal” becomes ordinary

Disk degeneration 68% · bulge 50% · protrusion 33% · annular fissure 22%. Most of the bars climb together now. That is aging shifting the background, not injury.

AGE 50

The scan accumulates words

Disk degeneration 80% · bulge 60% · protrusion 36% · annular fissure 23%. A longer report still does not name the source of your pain.

AGE 60

Most discs look different

Disk degeneration 88% · bulge 69% · protrusion 38% · annular fissure 25%. The overlay tracks how common a finding is, not how much it hurts.

AGE 70

The base rate dominates

Disk degeneration 93% · bulge 77% · protrusion 40% · annular fissure 27%. A finding can be real and still need the history and exam to mean anything.

AGE 80

Near saturation

Disk degeneration 96% · bulge 84% · protrusion 43% · annular fissure 29%. The scan is detailed. What caused the pain still belongs to the history and the examination.

Watch the “abnormalities” arrive.

Each card is one line a radiologist might write. Flip it, and the scary vocabulary becomes a base rate: how often the same feature shows up in people with no back pain.

An “abnormal” MRI is the normal result.

NORMAL
FOR AGE
About the mock reportIt sums the four group prevalences to estimate an average count. It does not assume the findings are independent and never calculates a joint probability.
The curve

The gray hair of the spine

Four model-predicted prevalence curves. Tap a label to isolate a finding. The source only reports decade values, so we joined them with straight lines.

Percent of asymptomatic individuals · Brinjikji et al., AJNR 2015, Table 2.

The words

“Degeneration” and “bulge” are descriptions.

Radiology needs words for shape, signal, and wear. Those words can be useful without being a verdict on pain. Brinjikji and colleagues concluded1: “Many imaging-based degenerative features are likely part of normal aging and unassociated with pain…”

Jensen’s 1994 echo2: among 98 people without back pain, 52% had a disk bulge at at least one level and 27% had a protrusion.

So don't toss the scan. Use it for a different question: does this finding fit the history, examination, and neurologic pattern?

Language ≠ mechanismA structural finding can matter, be incidental, or sit inside a bigger pain process. Only context decides which.
Words vs. meaning

Decode the report

Three common phrases, translated in plain words.

Degenerative disc disease
Wear visible on scan
96% of pain-free 80-year-olds: disk degeneration
Disc bulge
The disc extends broadly beyond its usual margin
50% of pain-free 40-year-olds
Annular fissure
A line or separation in the disc’s outer ring
29% of pain-free 80-year-olds
Counterweight

Painful spines are not identical.

Most findings are common, but some still track with pain. A companion meta-analysis in adults 50 or younger found disc bulge, disc degeneration, extrusion and protrusion, Modic type 1 change, and spondylolysis enriched in painful spines. Annular fissure (OR 1.79, P=.06) and spondylolisthesis (OR 1.59, P=.20) missed statistical significance. The review is published as an abstract only, so this stays preliminary, awaiting expert verification.

The takeawayBase rates keep you from overcalling. Association data keep you from dismissing everything. Neither replaces the patient in front of you.
The overuse stake

Early MRI travels with more care

In observational data on uncomplicated low back pain, an early MRI was associated with markedly higher costs and more surgery.

Total costs

OBSERVATIONAL ASSOCIATION, NOT CAUSATION.

Red flags

Do not scan every back. Do not miss the dangerous one.

ACR guidance3: for uncomplicated acute low back pain, no imaging for the first six weeks. The timeline changes when any of these show up:

  • Suspicion of cancer
  • Suspicion of infection
  • Cauda equina syndrome or other severe neurologic compromise
  • Fracture

Severe or progressive neurologic deficits, and symptoms that persist despite appropriate management, also change the timeline and the imaging strategy.

Not a checklist diagnosisRed flags guide clinical evaluation. Individual features vary in accuracy and must be interpreted together.
Educational reference

Four reasons to change course

No quiz, score, or symptom checker, just plain-language reasons clinicians may image urgently.

Red flags are uncommon. That’s why they matter.

Educational only; talk to a clinician.

Reporting

What if the report carried its own context?

The LIRE trial4 (NCT02015455) tested a simple fix: print age-specific prevalence benchmarks for common findings right inside lumbar imaging reports. Instead of leaving “bulge” alone on the page, the report shows how often it appears in people without pain.

LIRENCT02015455

Some systems now print these age-expected numbers inside radiology reports, putting epidemiology beside anatomy at the moment decisions begin.

Your MRI isn’t lying about your spine. It’s just not telling you about your pain.

Context is an interventionNumbers can change how a report is read without changing a single pixel of the scan.

Notes

Superscript numbers in the essay point here.

  1. Brinjikji W, et al. Systematic Literature Review of Imaging Features of Spinal Degeneration in Asymptomatic Populations. AJNR. 2015;36:811-816. Table 2 supplies the age-prevalence series; four of the eight findings are shown here. ↩
  2. Jensen MC, et al. Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Lumbar Spine in People Without Back Pain. NEJM. 1994;331:69-73. Among 98 people without back pain, 52% had a disk bulge at one or more levels. ↩
  3. ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Low Back Pain. For uncomplicated acute low back pain, no imaging for the first six weeks absent red flags. ↩
  4. Lumbar Imaging Reporting with Epidemiology (LIRE), NCT02015455. Trial testing age-specific prevalence benchmarks printed inside lumbar imaging reports. ↩
Sources

What these numbers can and cannot say

  • These are cross-sectional group prevalences, not individual predictions.
  • “Asymptomatic” was defined heterogeneously across 33 studies: 32 MRI studies and 1 CT study.
  • Finding severity was not stratified in the age-prevalence table.
  • Slider values between decades are linear interpolations added for this visualization.
  • Overuse figures are observational associations, not proof that early MRI caused later care.
  • Chart data: the four age-prevalence series are in data/mri-back-pain/.
  1. Brinjikji W, et al. Systematic Literature Review of Imaging Features of Spinal Degeneration in Asymptomatic Populations. AJNR. 2015;36:811 to 816. Table 2 supplies the age-prevalence series; four of the eight findings are shown here.
  2. Jensen MC, et al. Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Lumbar Spine in People Without Back Pain. NEJM. 1994;331:69 to 73.
  3. Brinjikji W, et al. MRI Findings of Disc Degeneration Are More Prevalent in Adults with Low Back Pain than in Asymptomatic Controls. AJNR. 2015. Only the abstract was checked for the preliminary counterweight panel.
  4. ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Low Back Pain. Imaging timing and red-flag indications.
  5. Lumbar Imaging Reporting with Epidemiology (LIRE), NCT02015455.
  6. An image-based review of the ACR Appropriateness Criteria for Low Back Pain. Observational early-imaging cost and surgery figures.

Draft for expert medical review. Educational, not medical advice; talk to a clinician. Seek urgent care for new bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle-area numbness, rapidly progressive weakness, or other concerning symptoms.

Essay 02 · Animated epidemiology
Draft for expert review

The typical spinal cord injury patient is 15 years older than in 1973.

By Jonathan Byrne, DO · October 2026

Why this essay: Spinal cord injury is the heart of physiatry, and its demographics shifted while nobody was looking.

Surviving the injury was only the first change. The patients got older, the causes tilted toward falls, and the rehab system built around the young trauma patient has not caught up.

1972 → 2025

Scrub five decades of Model Systems data, isolate the causes, and measure the missing years after injury.

SCROLL THROUGH THE COHORTS ↓

In 1973, a spinal cord injury was a young man’s car crash.

28.7mean age at injury, 1972 to 79

The hook

The patient moved fifteen years to the right.

You might be thinking that number sounds high for this injury. Across nine year-of-injury cohorts, mean age at injury rose to 43.2. A newer data-sheet window, “since 2015” through August 2025, puts the current anchor at 44.3. That anchor is related, but it is not a tenth point in the older cohort series.

The clinical version: a rehab system built around the young trauma patient increasingly meets a middle-aged or older adult, often after a fall.

A sampled historyThe National SCI Database follows patients treated at SCI Model Systems centers. It is not a census of every U.S. injury.
The fifty-year morph

Fifty years of spinal cord injury, scrolling past.

First-year survival improved since the 1970s. After the first year, life expectancy has not changed since the early 1980s. The dashboard draws direction only; it invents no intermediate points.

Etiology crossover

Falls nearly caught car crashes.

Falls kept climbing while crashes kept sliding. Crashes still lead, but a 30.4-point gap narrowed to just 4.6 points.

You would expect the aging to show up everywhere, and it nearly does: Chen and colleagues3 found it across sex, race, and every cause except violence. People injured through violence stayed young.

Since the 1970s, first-year life expectancy for people with tSCI improved steadily. For those who survived that first year, life expectancy has not budged since the early 1980s, and it still sits below the general population.

Notes

Superscript numbers in the essay point here.

Methodology & sources

What the database can and cannot say

  • Model Systems sample: these era trends describe patients treated at federally funded SCI Model Systems centers, not a complete national registry. A 2013 factsheet estimated roughly 13% capture. Scene deaths are excluded.
  • Separate national estimates: incidence comes from Jain et al. 2015; prevalence from Lasfargues et al. 1995. They are not counts from the Model Systems database.
  • Cohort definitions changed over time: 1972-79 through 2015-21 cohorts come from the 2021 Annual Statistical Report. "Since 2015" anchors use a still-growing window through August 2025 and are shown separately.
  • Complication categories changed: medical/surgical complications were separated from "Other" in later reporting.
  • Life expectancy: period estimates from the 2026 Data Sheet, awaiting expert cross-check.
  • Stylized distribution: timeline means are exact; the histogram's shape is illustrative.
  • Chart data: era anchors and cause shares are in data/sci-cohort/.

Essay 03 · Sports epidemiology
Draft pending expert review

Is pickleball actually dangerous?

By Jonathan Byrne, DO · October 2026

Why this essay: Everyone suddenly plays pickleball, and the ER numbers looked scarier than they were.

Emergency visits nearly doubled. Admissions more than tripled. But the per-player line barely moved.

A seven-beat data story

Follow the boom from player counts to falls, wrists, admissions, and costs, then meet the denominator that changes the headline.

SCROLL TO RETURN SERVE ↓

Every boom has a fracture curve.

5.7×more U.S. players, 2019→2024
+91%ED injuries, 2020→2022
+257%hospital admissions, 2020→2022
The boom
Serve

Pickleball grew from 3.46 million players to 19.81 million.

In 2019, pickleball was already shaking off the retirement-community stereotype. Five years later, the SFIA survey counted 19.81 million U.S. players, up 45.8% in a single year and the fastest-growing sport four years running.

And yes, that denominator is loose: SFIA counts anyone age six or older who played even once that year. These are survey estimates, not registrations or regular players.

Source: SFIA 2025 Topline Participation Report4. Annual series used here: 3.46M, 4.20M, 4.82M, 8.95M, 13.58M, 19.81M.
The curve

Divide by players and the scary line goes flat.

Two different scales, two lines rising together. Injury estimates are shown only for the verified Cheng endpoints.

Toggle between absolute growth and the per-player rate, and watch what happens to the scary line.

2020
8,894 ÷ 4.20M
= 2.1 / 1,000→2022
16,997 ÷ 8.95M
= 1.9 / 1,000

The headline is true.

Nationally estimated ED injuries rose from 8,894 in 2020 to 16,997 in 2022, a 91% jump. The series dipped 14% in 2020, then climbed 41% into 2021. That dip is a pandemic closure artifact, not proof the sport briefly got safer.

12

Participation rose faster.

Over the same endpoint years, SFIA’s player estimate more than doubled: 4.20 million to 8.95 million. The injury curve is real, and so is the growth curve underneath it.

SFIA survey series; Cheng NEISS estimates.

Divide by players.

Divide injuries by players and the explosion flattens to about two ED visits per 1,000 players per year: 2.1 in 2020, 1.9 in 2022.

Our derived calculation · not a published finding

Flat is not precise.

NEISS misses urgent care, office, PT, and self-managed injuries, while SFIA counts one-time players. The early injury estimates carry wide uncertainty. “Roughly flat” is the strongest claim these mismatched denominators can support.

The line the data supportsPickleball did not clearly become more dangerous per player. There were simply far more players available to get hurt.
Who gets hurt
Rally

The growth belongs to everyone. The ED curve skews older.

Cheng’s patients averaged 63.9 years old, and 73% of injuries fell in ages 60 through 79. A separate 10-year analysis put 61.1% between 65 and 80. Different bins, same signal.

The pale bars mark bins without published data, not values. The red span shows only the verified combined share.

Enter an age to highlight the matching band. This is descriptive only, never an individual risk estimate.

How it happens
Rally

First you lose your footing. Then your hand meets the court.

Falls caused 65.5% of injuries in Yu’s 2013 to 2022 series and 63.3% among seniors in Weiss’s 2010 to 2019 series. What follows is classic FOOSH: a fall onto an outstretched hand.

65.5%FALLS · YU ET AL. 2025

Who fractures? Who sprains?

WOMENMEN

fracture / sprain shareYu et al. 20252

You might be thinking this is everyone’s injury, but 69.1% of all fractures happened in women. In Weiss’s senior-only study, women had 9.3× the odds of wrist fracture versus men (95% CI 3.6 to 23.9). Those are ED-presentation odds, not population risk.

Sources: 2 3
Where it breaks

The wrist takes the hit.

In Yu’s series, the wrist was the single most injured body part: 12.7% of all injuries and 29.2% of all fractures. Fractures clustered in the upper body; sprains clustered below the waist.

12.7%

Wrist

The most frequently injured body part. It accounted for 29.2% of all fractures, the clearest trace of the FOOSH mechanism.

2 · ED presentations only.
Severity

Visits nearly doubled. Admissions more than tripled.

Hospital admissions rose from an estimated 992 in 2020 to 3,541 in 2022. After adjusting for sex, injury type, and site, being 65 or older carried 2.48 times the odds of admission.

992
2020
3,541
2022 · +257%
2.48×odds of hospital admission, age ≥65 vs <65
95% CI 1.54 to 4.11 · P<.001

Most patients still went home: earlier series reported 83 to 88% treated and released.

1. Absolute admission counts are national estimates, not raw cases.
Match point

The fracture curve is a participation curve.

An active older population doesn’t need to go back to the couch. It needs safer entry into the sport: equipment that matches the court, preparation that matches the movement, and a health plan that matches the player.

One more case-definition trapAmong senior pickleball cases in Weiss et al., 11.1% were cardiovascular non-injuries. NEISS records medical events linked to the activity; not every case is a musculoskeletal injury.

So is pickleball dangerous? Sort of. Mostly it’s crowded.

Methodology & sources

What this curve can and cannot say

  • ED visits only: NEISS does not see urgent care, office, physical therapy, or self-managed injuries.
  • Weighted estimates: national numbers come from a probability sample; early pickleball years have wide confidence intervals.
  • Different studies, different case definitions: Yu excluded 11,629 nationally estimated cardiac, heat, and non-musculoskeletal cases from its mechanism analysis; Cheng and Weiss used different windows and classifications.
  • Survey denominator: SFIA participation is based on about 20,000 online interviews, ages 6+, and counts at least one play per year.
  • Derived rate: the 2.1 and 1.9 per 1,000 figures divide Cheng’s NEISS endpoints by SFIA participation. They are our calculations, not published incidence rates.
  • The 2020 dip: the 14% fall in 2020 reflects disrupted access and play, not a modeled safety improvement.
  • Player-base contrast: SFIA reported ages 25 to 34 as the largest 2023 cohort at 2.3M; a full comparable age distribution is not supplied, so only the reported cohort is shown.
  • Chart data: the participation series, ED endpoints, and age anchors used here are in data/pickleball-fracture-curve/.

Did carbon-plate shoes really break the marathon?

By Jonathan Byrne, DO · October 2026

Why this essay: I’m a marathon runner who watched the record fall and wanted the lab numbers behind it.

One shoe made running four percent cheaper, metabolically speaking. Nine years later, the two-hour marathon fell in a real race. This is what the shoe actually did, and where the telling usually goes off the rails.

The fastest marathon ever run was not a record.

In 2019, Eliud Kipchoge ran 1:59:40.2 in the Ineos run, with rotating pacers and lab-like conditions. It proved a human could break two hours. It was not a ratified race, so it never entered the record books.

Seven years later, the barrier fell for real. Sabastian Sawe ran 1:59:30 in London on April 26, 2026, in legal shoes, in a real race: ten seconds faster than the run that did not count.1

One treadmill test made running 4% cheaper.

Picture the setup: 18 elite men on a Colorado treadmill, running 14, 16, and 18 km/h in three mass-matched racing shoes. The Vaporfly prototype burned 4.16% less energy than the Nike Streak 6 and 4.01% less than the adidas Adios Boost 2. Both gaps cleared statistical muster (p<0.001).2

Hoogkamer et al. (2018) was funded by Nike, and two co-authors worked at the Nike Sport Research Lab; later independent analyses found the same direction of benefit.

Every runner in the study improved, which is striking. But look at who they were: fast men in their twenties, all wearing size 10, all on a treadmill. “Four percent” is a lab average, not a guarantee stamped on your receipt.

Four percent cheaper in the lab. What is that on the clock?

Make it personal: move the slider to your marathon best and watch the lab number turn into clock time. The verdict line reads it back in plain words.

95.84
relative units
−4.16%energetic cost
≈2.6 to 3.4%modeled velocity gain
4:41modeled time saved at 2.6%
6:07modeled time saved at 3.4%

Model estimate, not a guarantee. Kipp et al. convert a 4% economy gain into roughly 2.6 to 3.4% faster velocity at marathon pace; air resistance and individual response matter.3

Running economy is fuel burn.

Here is what the lab actually measured: the energy needed to hold one fixed speed. The prototype just made that pace cheaper to run.

The clock moves less.

You might be thinking: 4% cheaper, so 4% faster? Not quite. Kipp’s models translate the economy gain into roughly 2.6 to 3.4% more marathon speed.

Move the personal best.

Use the slider. The display applies that velocity band to a finishing time. It is a modeled range, not a performance prediction.

The street test pointed the same way.

The New York Times Upshot dug through thousands of paired Strava race records, including runners who raced the same events in different shoes. Runners in the new shoes ran 4 to 5% faster than in average shoes, and 1.5 to 2.5% faster than in the next-best shoe.4

It is observational: it cannot fully control training, weather, the course, who reports which shoe, or who even uses Strava. But it pointed the same direction as the lab.5

The record line broke when the shoes arrived.

Drag the record-year slider (or just scroll) and watch the marks fall. Look for the hollow dot at 1:59:40: a run that happened but was never a record.6

Pre-super-shoeVaporfly · 2017WA rules · 2020Current
SCROLL-DRIVEN RECORD LINE5 / 5
1:59:30

Sabastian Sawe · London · April 26, 2026 · first sub-2:00 marathon in a ratified race

2003 to 2014

The line barely moved.

Paula Radcliffe’s 2:15:25 stood for 16 years. Dennis Kimetto ran 2:02:57 in Berlin in 2014, back when shoes were just shoes.

2018 to 2023

Then the curve broke.

Then Kipchoge chipped the men’s mark down to 2:01:39 (2018) and 2:01:09 (2022). Kiptum took it to 2:00:35 in 2023; he died in February 2024 at age 24.

2019 · ghost run

1:59:40.2 was not a record.

Kipchoge’s 2019 Ineos run used rotating pacers and lab-like conditions. It proved a human could do it, but it was not a ratified race.

APRIL 26, 2026

The barrier fell for real.

Sawe ran 1:59:30 in London, with Kejelcha (1:59:41) and Kiplimo (2:00:28) right behind him. Three men under the old record in a single race.

The shoe is not the whole story.

World Athletics stepped in in January 2020, effective April 30, with road-shoe limits: 40 mm maximum stack and no more than one rigid plate. That July it set track-spike limits at 20 mm for events up to 800 m and 25 mm above 800 m. Kipchoge’s Ineos shoe was reported at roughly 50 mm with multiple plates, which would fail today’s limits outright. Current models must also sit on retail shelves for at least four months, and approved shoes can be inspected during record ratification.7

The plate got the name, but the foam may do as much work. The original prototype changed foam, stack height, plate, and geometry all at once, so the plate’s solo contribution was never cleanly isolated; reviews suggest the foam may contribute as much as the plate, or more. The 2016-to-2026 change was a whole system: lower stack and conventional foam with no plate became 40 mm of resilient foam, one curved plate, and rocker geometry.8

Not everyone gets four percent. A September 2026 summary compared the top 50 road performances from 2009 to 2015 against 2017 to 2024, using throwing events as an era-wide control: women’s performances improved 4.51% against 2.62% for men, with throws near 1%. Possibly women’s records simply had more room to move; that is an interpretation, not a settled biological effect.9

The evidence on injury points both ways. Worth watching: lower cadence and more rearfoot eversion in advanced footwear; five case reports of navicular bone stress injuries in elite runners; surveys report ankle, Achilles, and plantar-fascia symptoms, though surveys cannot prove causation. Reassuring: lower ankle plantarflexion moments in the same 2026 PM&R study of 23 elite runners; a 2025 study found reduced muscle and joint forces; no increase in Achilles loading and no consistent plate effect on joint power or leg stiffness. No published study has measured actual injury rates in super-shoe versus conventional-shoe cohorts.10

The shoes are proven to make you faster. Nothing has proven they break you, or that they do not.

1:59:30

Legal shoes. A real race. The revolution won.

Sawe’s 1:59:30 needed no asterisks: legal shoes, a real race, and ten seconds faster than Kipchoge’s unofficial Ineos run.

Notes

Superscript numbers in the essay point here. Each note gives the source and says plainly where the figure comes from.

  1. Record marks are from World-Athletics-recognized race reporting, current through October 2026. Kipchoge’s 1:59:40.2 (2019 Ineos run) used rotating pacers and is not a ratified record. Chepngetich’s 2:09:56 record stands; she was suspended in July 2025 after a failed drug test. Assefa’s women-only record is 2:15:41, London 2026. ↩
  2. Hoogkamer W et al. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(4):1009 to 1019. DOI 10.1007/s40279-017-0811-2. n=18 elite men; mass-matched shoes; 14/16/18 km/h on a treadmill; all wore size 10. ↩
  3. Kipp S, Kram R, Hoogkamer W. Frontiers in Physiology. 2019;10:79. DOI 10.3389/fphys.2019.00079. The 2.6 to 3.4% velocity band is model-dependent; air resistance and individual response matter. ↩
  4. Quealy K, Katz J. NYT Upshot, July 2018 and Dec. 13, 2019. Paired Strava race records; observational, self-selected runners. ↩
  5. Guinness J et al., arXiv:2002.06105 (2020). Independent analysis with photo-identified footwear. ↩
  6. Timeline dots are ratified marks only; the hollow dot is Kipchoge’s unofficial 1:59:40.2. Shoes are era classifications; model-by-model footwear is not always officially documented. ↩
  7. Jan. 31, 2020 amendment, effective Apr. 30; July 28, 2020 track amendment. Dates and dimensions are secondary-sourced from reporting of the World Athletics amendments; the current official rulebook was not checked. ↩
  8. Mechanism synthesis: Hoogkamer W, Kipp S, Kram R. Sports Medicine. 2019;49:133 to 143. DOI 10.1007/s40279-018-1024-z. The plate’s solo contribution was never cleanly isolated in the original experiment. ↩
  9. Sept. 2026 MarathonHandbook summary comparing top-50 road performances (2009 to 2015 vs 2017 to 2024) with throwing events as a control. The full paper has not been checked; preliminary. ↩
  10. Concern: Bruneau MM, Gaudette LW, et al. PM&R. Apr. 23, 2026. DOI 10.1002/pmrj.70153. n=23 (11 women, 12 men); biomechanical proxies, not injuries. Counter-evidence: Scientific Reports. 2025;15:17828. DOI 10.1038/s41598-025-03029-0. No published study has measured actual injury rates in super-shoe versus conventional-shoe cohorts. ↩
  11. Real professional runners at the 2025 Berlin Marathon, Wikimedia Commons; linked in the caption. No generated athlete or shoe imagery is used. ↩

Methods

Lab figures come from Hoogkamer et al. (2018): 18 elite men, treadmill, mass-matched shoes. The 2.6 to 3.4% velocity band is Kipp et al.’s model (2019), not a measurement. Street figures come from the NYT Upshot’s paired-Strava analysis (2018, 2019) and Guinness et al.’s photo-identified study (2020); both are observational. Records are World-Athletics-recognized marks through October 2026. Rules come from secondary reporting of the 2020 World Athletics amendments. The women’s 4.51% vs 2.62% figures come from a September 2026 MarathonHandbook summary whose full paper has not been checked. Injury evidence is biomechanical proxies, five case reports, and surveys; no cohort injury-rate study exists. The converter multiplies your entered time by the velocity band; it models a range, not a prediction. The record line connects ratified marks only, and the hollow dot is Kipchoge’s unofficial 1:59:40.2. Chart data: data/carbon-plate-revolution/. Draft pending expert review.

Essay 05 · Exercise physiology Draft pending expert review

Why does a humid 75°F morning feel so bad?

By Jonathan Byrne, DO · October 2026

Why this essay: I train in South Florida humidity, and the thermometer kept lying to me.

A humid 75°F morning can feel worse than a dry 90°F afternoon. The dew point, not the temperature or the humidity percentage, decides how well your sweat can cool you.

SCROLL INTO THE MUGGY AIR ↓

Make your own weather.

Drag the sliders to build any morning, then type in your easy pace. Watch the dew point write the verdict on your run.1

ATMOSPHERE INPUT
Magnus-Tetens: b=17.625, c=243.04°C. Heat index uses the NWS Rothfusz regression and appears only at ≥80°F.1
72°F DEW POINT
the thermometer lags behind the air
Very humid. Cooling is constrained.

Expect sweat to linger and effort to rise. Use effort, not a rigid pace, as your primary guide.

TEMP + DEW POINT147
HEAT INDEX-
PACE ADJUSTMENT4.5%
YOUR ADJUSTED EASY PACE9:24/mi

The pace-adjustment percentage comes from a coach's rule of thumb: Mark Hadley8's 2013 temperature-plus-dew-point bands, not a peer-reviewed lab study. Treat it as a cue to back off effort, not a prescription.8

DAY A · COOLER / SATURATED75°F

90% relative humidity

72°F dew point
DAY B · HOTTER / DRIER95°F

40% relative humidity · heat index ≈99°F

67°F dew point

Day A is cooler. Its air is closer to saturation.

The hotter day is obviously brutal. But the dew point catches something the thermometer and the heat index miss. The cooler morning leaves less room for your sweat to evaporate.

Relative humidity is actual vapor pressure divided by the saturation vapor pressure at the current temperature.2 Warm air holds far more water vapor, so the percentage shifts as the temperature shifts, even when the air gains no moisture. Dew point is the temperature at which that air would hit saturation: when the dew point climbs, the moisture content climbed with it. One humidity number cannot tell you how a run will feel: the same 70% relative humidity can describe a pleasant 55°F morning or a punishing 85°F one.

Dew points computed with Magnus-Tetens.1 This comparison does not claim Day A is more dangerous overall.10
SAME READING70% RH

At 55°F, dew point is ≈45°F: cool air holding relatively little moisture.

SAME READING70% RH

At 85°F, dew point is ≈74°F: warm air loaded with water vapor.

DAY A · 75°F · DEW POINT 72°F
DAY B · 95°F · DEW POINT 67°F
6:00 AM · SAME CLOCK, DIFFERENT AIR

Sweat only cools you when it leaves.

Evaporation runs on the vapor-pressure gap between wet skin and the air around you. The 95°F anchor sits within the textbook 34 to 36°C exercising mean3-skin-temperature range.3 The closer the dew point sits to skin temperature, the less gradient escaping vapor has. Sweat stays on the skin while heart rate and thermal strain climb. Day A's air sits closer to saturation than Day B's, so its gap is narrower even though the day is cooler.

DAY A · 75°F / 90% RH

95 − 72 = 23°F GAP

Narrower gap. Same sweat, less cooling.

DAY B · 95°F / 40% RH

95 − 67 = 28°F GAP

Wider gap. More room for vapor to escape.

In Miami, summer is four months of heavy air.

NOAA's 1991 to 20206 normals for Miami International Airport put the average dew point at 72.0°F in June, 73.0°F in July, 73.8°F in August, and 73.2°F in September.6 That is four straight months parked in the runner's "very humid" band.

JAN
FEB

APR
MAY
72.0JUN
73.0JUL
73.8AUG
73.2SEP
OCT
NOV
DEC

Only the four verified summer-month normals are filled; other months are intentionally left unquantified. NOAA 1991 to 2020 normals, Miami International Airport.

72 to 74°F

Miami’s average dew point from June through September. NWS Miami calls dew point “the best measure of moisture levels in Florida.”

NWS Miami summer-season climatology.
162 → 8%

A typical August morning at 88°F with a 74°F dew point sums to 162, Hadley’s 161 to 170 pace-adjustment band. Treat the 8% as a cue to back off effort, not a physiological law.8

NWS Miami calls dew point "the best measure of moisture levels in Florida."2 NWS Miami summer-season climatology.

They sweated the same and got less cooling.

Che Muhamed4 and colleagues randomized 11 trained male distance runners across five treadmill sessions at 31°C (87.8°F): 60 minutes at 70% VO₂max, then an incremental test to volitional exhaustion.4

Time to exhaustion dropped significantly at 61% and 71% relative humidity versus 23% (P=0.045 and P=0.005). Mean body temperature ran higher, and heart rate and stroke volume shifted. But whole-body sweat loss did not differ (P=0.183).

Performance signal by condition

Flip the toggle to re-plot the same five conditions by dew point instead of relative humidity. The story does not change: at the same 88°F air temperature, the endpoints span ≈45°F to ≈77°F dew point.

Bar heights are categorical emphasis, not unreported time-to-exhaustion values. Dew points are our Magnus-Tetens computations. Limits: n=11 trained men; laboratory treadmill protocol; one air temperature; TTE test rather than road race.

Marathon times slow in warm, wet air, and slower runners bend most.

Ely and colleagues pulled together decades of results from seven marathons and sorted race weather into four WBGT quartiles, from 5.1 to 10°C up to 20.1 to 25°C.5 Top men slowed 1.7%, 2.5%, 3.3%, and 4.5% versus course-record pace across those quartiles. The slower finishing groups were hit harder.

WBGT vs slowdown
70%NATURAL WET-BULB
20%GLOBE
10%DRY-BULB

Who bends most?

The plotted values are the exact top-male figures. The original study found progressively larger slowdowns in slower finishers, though exact quartile values are not reproduced here.

Ely modeled WBGT and temperature. The bridge is physical: outdoor WBGT is 70% natural wet-bulb, and wet-bulb is strongly governed by atmospheric moisture. Dew point was inside the index, not isolated as its own predictor.

The flag system already runs on WBGT, not humidity.

The classic ACSM9 Event Alert System runs on WBGT, not relative humidity.9 Below 50°F is white for hypothermia risk. 50 to 64°F is green. At 65 to 72°F, at-risk runners should slow. At 73 to 82°F, at-risk runners should withdraw and others should slow. Above 82°F WBGT is black: cancel or recommend voluntary withdrawal.

Those are 2007 race-day thresholds. ACSM's 2023 exertional-heat-illness consensus is the current clinical reference. It covers environmental heat stress, activity modification, recognition, rapid cooling, and individualized return.

Air temperature plus dew point alone cannot validly assign an ACSM flag. Use an on-site or race-reported WBGT.

WHITE<50°F

Hypothermia risk

GREEN50 to 64°F

Decreased risk

YELLOW65 to 72°F

At-risk runners slow down

RED73 to 82°F

At-risk withdraw; others slow

BLACK>82°F

Cancel or voluntary withdrawal

The chart every runner knows, and where it came from.

The familiar runner's dew-point chart traces to a letsrun.com7 forum thread from about 1995, not a laboratory validation study.7 Its breakpoints line up broadly with meteorological guidance. Around 55°F feels comfortable, above 65°F feels humid, and above 75°F feels oppressive. The agreement makes the chart plausible; its origin is still a forum thread, not a lab study.

Coach Mark Hadley's 2013 rule adds air temperature and dew point, then assigns adjustments from 0.5% at 101 to 110 to 10% at 171 to 180.8 A 2026 preprint describes the bands explicitly as "not peer-reviewed physiology." An effort-based decision beats treating 8% like a biological constant.

≤54°FDry to very comfortable
55 to 64°FComfortable to okay for most
65 to 69°FA bit uncomfortable for most
70 to 74°FVery humid; quite uncomfortable
≥75°FExtremely uncomfortable

The calculator at the top of this essay applies Hadley's bands to whatever weather you build. Same arithmetic, same caveat.

Check the dew point. Run the effort the air will allow.

Notes

Superscript numbers in the essay point here. Each note names the source and says plainly where the figure comes from.

  1. All dew points on this page are computed from air temperature and relative humidity with the Magnus-Tetens approximation (b=17.625, c=243.04°C). The heat index uses the NWS Rothfusz regression and appears only at air temperatures of 80°F or above. ↩
  2. Definitions and interpretation follow National Weather Service2 guidance. NWS Miami's summer-season climatology calls dew point "the best measure of moisture levels in Florida." ↩
  3. The 95°F skin anchor sits within the textbook 34 to 36°C exercising mean-skin-temperature range and remains pending expert confirmation. ↩
  4. Che Muhamed et al., Temperature, 2016. DOI 10.1080/23328940.2016.1182669. Eleven trained male distance runners; randomized treadmill sessions at 31°C: 60 minutes at 70% VO₂max, then an incremental test to volitional exhaustion. Time to exhaustion fell at 61% and 71% relative humidity versus 23% (P=0.045 and P=0.005); whole-body sweat loss did not differ (P=0.183). One air temperature; laboratory treadmill protocol, not a road race. ↩
  5. Ely et al., Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2008. DOI 10.1249/mss.0b013e31802d3aba. Decades of results from seven marathons, grouped by WBGT quartile, not dew point. The dew-point bridge is an interpretation: outdoor WBGT is 70% natural wet-bulb, which is strongly governed by atmospheric moisture. ↩
  6. Miami values are NOAA 1991 to 2020 climate normals for Miami International Airport: June 72.0, July 73.0, August 73.8, September 73.2°F. The other eight months are intentionally left unquantified. ↩
  7. The runner's dew-point comfort chart traces to a letsrun.com forum thread from about 1995 (thread 3139849), not a validation study; its breakpoints line up broadly with NOAA/NWS conventions. ↩
  8. The pace rule is coach Mark Hadley's 2013 temperature-plus-dew-point bands: 0.5% at a sum of 101 to 110, up to 10% at 171 to 180. A 2026 preprint describes the bands explicitly as "not peer-reviewed physiology": a cue to back off effort, not a prescription. ↩
  9. Flag thresholds are the classic 2007 ACSM Event Alert System. The 2023 ACSM exertional-heat-illness consensus is the current clinical reference. ↩
  10. Day A (75°F/90% RH) versus Day B (95°F/40% RH) shows that dew point detects evaporative constraint the thermometer misses; it does not claim the cooler morning is more dangerous overall. The heat index appears only for Day B because the regression is not valid below 80°F. ↩

Methods

How this was built. Every dew point on this page is computed from air temperature and relative humidity with the Magnus-Tetens approximation; the heat index uses the NWS Rothfusz regression and appears only at 80°F or above. The two peer-reviewed studies are Che Muhamed and colleagues (Temperature, 2016): 11 trained men on treadmills at 31°C, 60 minutes at 70% VO2max then an incremental test to exhaustion, and Ely and colleagues (Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2008), decades of results from seven marathons grouped by WBGT quartile, which captures moisture through its 70% wet-bulb weighting rather than isolating dew point. Miami's June to September averages are NOAA 1991 to 2020 climate normals for Miami International Airport; the other eight months were left blank because only those four were verified. The runner comfort bands and the temperature-plus-dew-point pace rule are coaching heuristics, not peer-reviewed physiology. The flag thresholds are the classic 2007 ACSM Event Alert System; the 2023 ACSM exertional-heat-illness consensus is the current clinical reference. Day A versus Day B shows that dew point detects evaporative constraint the thermometer misses; it does not claim the cooler morning is more dangerous overall. Draft under expert review; educational, not medical advice.

Walking is controlled falling.

By Jonathan Byrne, DO · October 2026 Draft for expert review

Why this essay: Gait is physiatry’s home turf: one second of walking contains the whole exam.

Scroll to walk it: the figure, clock, phase name, and joint readouts below all run from the same normative teaching values.2

You catch the fall twice per cycle.

In the Rancho Los Amigos / Perry convention, stance takes about 60% and swing about 40%.1 The part that keeps you upright is the overlap: two double-support windows of roughly 10% each, bookending single-limb support.

The knee makes the cycle’s biggest move while the foot is off the ground.

Tap a joint to isolate its curve, or tap a phase to jump the figure there. Watch the knee’s double bump: a small loading-response flexion, then a much larger swing peak of roughly 60°. The readout gives the plain version as you move.

0% · knee 3° flexed, the limb is set to accept your weight with the knee nearly straight

Curves interpolated between normative key values. The shape is representative, not one person’s recording.

INITIAL SWING

Meet Gus, a made-up walker who gets one thing wrong at each phase.

Gus is made up: a teaching dummy, not a patient. Walk him through the cycle and each phase breaks in exactly one place.

Drop foot

Loading response: Gus’s foot slaps the ground because his tibialis anterior cannot lower it eccentrically after contact. Swing: the same weakness means his toe drags, so he hikes his knee and hip to make clearance: the steppage pattern.

Trendelenburg

Midstance: Gus’s opposite hip drops because his gluteus medius cannot hold the pelvis level over the stance leg. He leans his trunk over the stance leg to cut the abductor demand.

These are illustrative teaching patterns, not diagnoses or a symptom checker. Similar observations can have many causes and need a complete examination.

Know the phases, and every PM&R clinic hallway is a gait lab.

You’ve been doing the most complex thing your nervous system does, ~5,000 times a day, on autopilot.

MID-SWING

A beautiful old theory tried to explain the smoothness.

In 1953, Saunders, Inman, and Eberhart proposed six mechanisms: pelvic rotation, pelvic tilt, knee flexion in stance, foot and ankle mechanisms, knee-ankle-foot interactions, and lateral pelvic displacement. Together they supposedly flatten the center-of-gravity path (~5 cm vertical and ~6 cm lateral) and make walking efficient.35 Later, Kirtley (1999) and Kerrigan and colleagues (2001) asked whether those mechanisms really minimize vertical displacement or explain efficiency.4 Charming idea; treat it as a historical lens, not current doctrine.

Notes

Superscript numbers in the essay point here. Each note gives the source and says plainly where the figure comes from.

  1. Phase timing and the eight phases follow the Rancho Los Amigos / Perry convention; other texts divide swing slightly differently. ↩
  2. Joint angles are normative teaching values in the Perry tradition. The figure and curves approximate them to about ±5°, and the curves interpolate linearly between the key values. ↩
  3. Saunders, Inman & Eberhart, J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1953;35-A:543 to 558: the six-mechanisms paper, shown here with the later critique. ↩
  4. Kirtley (1999) and Kerrigan and colleagues (2001) questioned whether the six determinants really minimize vertical center-of-mass displacement or explain walking efficiency; treat the determinants as a historical lens, not current doctrine. ↩
  5. About 5 cm of vertical and 6 cm of lateral center-of-gravity oscillation are classic Inman-tradition reference values. ↩

What this schematic can and cannot say

Methods in one paragraph, with the data.

The figure and curves run on normative teaching values in the Perry / Rancho Los Amigos tradition, with the eight phases and their boundaries from that convention. Joint angles approximate ±5°, and the curves interpolate linearly between key values: the shape is representative, not one person’s recording. Broad teaching averages put cadence at about 101 to 122 steps/min and step length at about 2.5 ft; they are intentionally not used to score this figure. The clinical patterns are illustrative teaching examples, not diagnoses: similar observations can have many causes and need a complete examination. This essay is about cycle mechanics, not gait speed, mortality, or risk prediction. Chart data and key values: data/gait-cycle/ (CSV plus a README with sources and transformations). Open expert-review checks: phase-boundary convention, kinematic values, and the drop-foot/Trendelenburg pairing. Draft for expert review. Educational content only, not medical advice.

Essay 06 · Gait analysis · Draft for expert review.

By Jonathan Byrne, DO · October 2026 · Essay 07

Why this essay: I’m a maker with a 3D printer, and the cost curve of printed prosthetics stopped me cold.

The $50 Hand

A carpenter's table-saw accident, a YouTube comment, and seventy pins on a map became a volunteer movement printing prosthetic hands for $50 in plastic against $40,000 devices. The cost-collapse story of 3D-printed prosthetics: what fifty dollars of filament can do, and where it falls short.

FIG. 02 · EXPLODED PARTS · NOT TO SCALE

Exploded patent-style diagram of a Cyborg Beast-style hand: the printed shell, the screws, the cords, the padding. Every part a garage or campus makerspace can source, and the whole bill of materials is fifty dollars of stuff. Diagram only, not an assembly manual.

Build log 01 · 2011-2013 · design

It started with a table saw and a YouTube comment

No company planned this, and no grant funded it. A carpenter who lost fingers, a puppeteer who knew how joints move, and a researcher who left a comment on a video built a volunteer manufacturing network by accident.

In 2011, South African carpenter Richard Van As teamed up with Bellingham special-effects artist and puppeteer Ivan Owen. They built a mechanical finger, then a hand.2

In February 2013, MakerBot donated two 3D printers; Owen and Van As released the first printable hand's design files open-source, public domain. Anyone with a printer could build one.3

That spring, RIT researcher Jon Schull saw the YouTube video and dropped a Google map mashup into the comments, inviting makers and recipients to pin themselves: 70 pins in 6 weeks. The Google+ community became e-NABLE.4

From 2014, a design boom: myoelectric versions, plus task-specific hands for bike-riding and trumpet-playing. One father built his son a hand with two thumbs ("Cool Hand Luke"). The map kept blooming because the files were free.

Older e-NABLE materials cite ~20,000 volunteers and 8,000 recipients; a recent partner page lists 197 chapters across 53 countries and ~33,000 volunteers. No audited count exists. Treat each figure as a dated organizational claim.5

Jose Delgado Jr. was born missing much of his left hand. His myoelectric prosthesis cost thousands of dollars and gripped weakly; his 3D-printed Cyborg Beast cost $50 in materials (printer sold separately) and worked better. He drives with it.1

Scroll through the three beats below and watch what happens to the $50 bar when it is drawn on the same scale as $40,000.

Materials cost, one hand (scroll to feel the scale)
Myoelectric prosthesis
$40,000+
Printed Cyborg Beast
$50
Reading the chartOn a linear scale, the $50 bar is less than a pixel wide. Scroll on.

FIG. 05 · PRICE TAGS · FIELD SKETCH

The most expensive option isn't the most functional one.

Thousands for weak grip; $50 in filament for the hand that worked better. Price and performance don't have to move together.

Now stretch the $40,000 bar.

That's 800× the materials cost of the printed hand. The orange $50 bar is there, thinner than your screen can draw. Top-end myoelectric/bionic devices exceed $30,000 to $40,000+ (Bebionic >$30k; private bionic arms up to £60k).

The catch, stated up front.

"$50" is materials only: filament, screws, cord. Printer sold separately. A printed hand competes on different terms entirely. Keep scrolling.

Build log 02 · 2014 · print

Fifty dollars of filament can't match a $40,000 prosthesis, but it can win the only contest that counts: getting worn

The printed hand is weaker by every laboratory measure. Its advantage is that a child will wear a superhero hand to school and leave the beige hook in a drawer. This essay is about what fifty dollars of filament can do, and where it falls short.

Build log 03 · the refit cycle · print

Kids outgrow a fitted prosthesis every 6 to 12 months; a printed one just gets reprinted

Children outgrow a fitted prosthesis every 6 to 12 months (UNM / Carrie Tingley Hospital), and a basic claw-type pediatric hand costs $700 to $10,000 to make, re-fitted on that cycle until age 18. A printed hand costs $30 to $50 in filament and gets reprinted at the next size.6

What-if recomputer · projection
Cost of one hand, age 5 to 18 (assumes refits every 12 months, constant prices, no insurance)

Pick a device price below and watch the lifetime bill from age 5 to 18 change.

$50$5k$10k$40k
$65013 devices × $50 · one childhood of hands for less than a single conventional fitting
Build log 04 · acceptance · test

Kids reject $10,000 hands. Then ask for a printed one.

Prosthesis rejection is one of rehab's quietest epidemics. Biddiss & Chau (2007) screened ~200 articles and found rejection rates in 40: 45% for body-powered and 35% for electric devices in children (26% / 23% in adults). Some body-powered hook studies reach 80 to 87%.7

And yet kids reject $10,000 devices at high rates, then ask for superhero-printed ones: a 2026 systematic review found customization increases acceptance and comfort.8 No published rejection rate exists yet for printed devices specifically; the pattern is inferred across two separate literatures, not measured directly.9

Rejection isn't about price. It's about identity. A beige hook that costs $10,000 signals disability. A blue Iron Man hand that costs $50 signals superhero. One gets left in a drawer; the other gets worn to school. The cheapest device wins on the only metric that matters: hours worn per day.

Build log 05 · mechanism · test

Just a wrist: no motors, no batteries

The classic e-NABLE designs are wrist-driven: non-elastic cords run along the palmar fingers like tendons. 20 to 30° of wrist flexion closes the fingers into a composite fist; dorsal elastic cords re-extend them. Without a palm and ≥30° of wrist motion, the mechanism has nothing to pull with.10

Wrist-flexion simulator: drag the slider (simplified diagram, not to scale)

Drag the wrist slider from 0° to 30° and watch the fingers close; the readout tells you the hand's state at each angle.

0°15°30°
Print recipe · Schull

~$40 · ~15 h · ~2 h

Materials, printer time, assembly: "like a big Lego kit." Other builds run ~20 h per hand (Tampa Bay); a palm alone can take 16 h.

11
Materials

PLA or ABS, cord, screws

PLA or ABS plastic, Chicago screws, 1 mm nylon cord, 1.5 mm elastic cord, Velcro, foam padding, dial tensioner. A hardware-store bill of materials.

Requirement

A palm and 30° of wrist

Without wrist motion there's no mechanism. These designs cannot serve wrist-disarticulation or higher amputations; the myoelectric designs are for those.

Build log 06 · makers · ship

The supply chain for a $50 hand is a garage and a campus makerspace

The supply chain for a $50 hand is a garage, a campus makerspace, and a father who refused the catalog. Four sketches:

Omaha · the researcher

Jorge Zuniga

Built the Cyborg Beast after his young son saw a conventional prosthesis and said: "Daddy, that hand is too real." So he designed one that looked like a toy.

Orlando · the students

Manero & Sparkman

UCF students who built their first arm on a kitchen table for under $350 for Alex Pring, born missing most of his right arm. The delivery, styled like Iron Man by Robert Downey Jr., went viral.

The recipient

Tilly Lockey

Fitted with a Deus Ex-themed bionic arm as a teenager: proof that when a device looks like something you chose, teenagers wear it instead of hiding it.

The remix

"Cool Hand Luke"

A father who built his son a hand with two thumbs, because when the design files are free, the prescription pad is optional.

Build log 07 · limits · test

What a printed hand can't do

Every claim below comes with its sample size, because here the sample size is the story.

X-Limb is the best-documented printed hand: 253 g, 21.5 N power grip; 45,000 grasp cycles without failure; $200 bill of materials. It passed the Activities Measure for Upper-Limb Amputees (AM-ULA).12 An adult man's peak grip is about 52 kg (~510 N); a woman's about 34 kg (Portuguese workers).13 X-Limb's 21.5 N is about 4% of the man's figure. Touch Hand 4 managed 30.4 N but only 50% grasp success across test objects, with a 4.5-second response time; in one transradial amputee, a printed pressure-sensored hand showed lower grip strength and dexterity than the conventional myoelectric.14 Zuniga and colleagues fitted the Cyborg Beast to 5 children (ages 3 to 10) for 6 months, with significant gains in active range of motion and forearm circumference, small n and no control group.15 A 2026 systematic review of 20 articles (2020 to 2025) found a trend toward myoelectric/sensorized printed designs, pinch grip most effective, customization increasing acceptance and comfort.8 No randomized trials of printed prostheses exist.16 A printed hand is a gross-grasp assistive tool.

PLA creeps: it deforms under sustained load and degrades with heat and UV. A printed hand is a consumable: it will not last a decade, which is why the price matters. Classic wrist-driven designs require a palm and ≥30° of wrist flexion; higher amputations need motors the $50 design doesn't have.

The sentence the movement survives on is the regulatory story: e-NABLE chapters position their hands as "experimental assistive devices, not medical devices." External limb components sit in FDA Class I (21 CFR 890.3420); the custom-device exemption skips premarket approval but not quality-system, reporting, or labeling rules. The movement is meanwhile walking toward the clinic it once routed around: Hero Arm (Open Bionics) became an FDA-registered Class I device; NHS England funded multi-grip prostheses for children from 2018; Limbitless ran an OHSU clinical trial (2021) and is pursuing FDA clearance for prescription and insurance coverage. Whether the "not a medical device" framing would survive a serious adverse event is untested.

Build log 08 · the fine print · ship

Printer sold separately

Every $50 figure in this essay is materials only. The printer, the volunteer's time, and the fitting expertise are real costs someone absorbs.

A $50 printed hand leaves the prosthetist in place and deletes the waiting: for authorization, for the next size, for a device a child will actually wear. The prescription of the future might be a file, a printer, and a follow-up appointment.

Build log · appendix B · methods

Methods

Cost figures are materials-only unless a device is labeled conventional: the $50 Cyborg Beast figure and the Delgado story come from 3D Printing Industry; $40,000+ reflects top-end myoelectric devices. The pediatric recomputer multiplies one device's price by the refits needed from age 5 to 18 at a fixed 12-month interval (13 refits), assuming constant prices and no insurance; it is a projection, not a bill. Grip figures are peak power-grip values: 510 N for the adult-male reference, 21.5 N for X-Limb, 30.4 N for Touch Hand 4. e-NABLE scale figures are dated organizational claims with no audited count. The 2026 systematic review is conference-proceedings evidence. Chart values are published as CSVs in data/fifty-dollar-hand/, with a README describing sources and transformations. Essay 08 · Exercise Physiology Draft for expert review

What happens to your body at every hour of a marathon?

By Jonathan Byrne, DO · October 2026

Why this essay: I’ve run marathons, and I wanted an hour-by-hour account of what the body actually goes through.

One marathon, told hour by hour: three runners, one race clock, and every physiological beat anchored to a published number.

Run the clock from 0:00 to 4:30.

Scroll, and the race clock runs. The dots move at their own paces: gold is Priya at 4:16/km, blue is Marcus at 6:24/km, red is Louise, who never reaches the finish. Watch where they separate.

0:00:00
Race clock · scroll to run it
The gun fires. The tanks are full.
A
B
C
MILE 00:00START · 0 KM
PriyaMarcusLouise

The gun fires. The tanks are full.

A carbohydrate-loaded runner starts with muscle glycogen around 150 to 200 mmol per kg of wet muscle, roughly double the normal-diet store. Everyone on the line carries the same fuel. What differs is the burn rate.

5
1:001:00~14 KM
PriyaMarcus

A liter gone.

After about 10 minutes of steady effort, heart rate climbs at a constant pace while stroke volume falls: cardiovascular drift. By 1:00, about 1 liter of sweat is gone (0.92 to 0.99 L/h in a warm marathon7), and the heart beats roughly 10 bpm faster than at the start; in lab heat, drift reached +15 bpm over 45 to 60 minutes. Runners replace only a fraction of their losses, and underestimate their own sweat loss by 42.5%. In hot, humid conditions the rate can hit 1.5 L/h; one elite winner in Dubai sweated 3.6 L/h and finished 9.8% lighter.

678910
1:301:30HALF · 21.1 KM
Priya

Halfway for Priya: half the tank gone.

Priya crosses halfway in 1:30. Carb-loaded runners burn about 5 mmol of glycogen per kg per km, so 21 km has cost roughly 105 mmol/kg, about half of loaded stores (~200). The math for the full distance: 5 × 42.2 ≈ 210 mmol/kg. The tank doesn't reach the finish. That is why the wall comes before mile 26, not at it.

1
2:182:08 to 2:29WALL ZONE · 30 to 35 KM
Priya

The wall zone, for Priya.

At 4:16/km, kilometers 30 to 35 arrive between 2:08 and 2:29. Glycogen is near depletion, and a metabolic model predicts the wall at mile 21 for runners at 80 to 95% of VO₂max. Priya's risk stays low. Sub-3:00 men hit the wall only 1.42% of the time, because 82% of them even-pace.

11124
3:003:00FINISH · PRIYA
Priya

Priya finishes.

3:00:00. About 3% lighter than at the start7. Even-paced, and the wall never arrived. That is the modal outcome for this tier, not the heroic exception.

74
3:453:30 to 4:00MEDICAL TENT
Louise

Louise is in the medical tent.

Louise didn't dehydrate. Louise overdrank.

You might be thinking the fix is simple: just drink more. For Louise, that was the problem. Weight gain during the race was the strongest predictor of hyponatremia, and 35% of the Boston field gained weight. 13% of finishers were hyponatremic (Na⁺ ≤135 mmol/L); 0.6% were critical (≤120). Fluid type (water vs. sports drink) didn't matter. Neither did sex or NSAIDs.

Louise is the exception. By 2:00, most runners had sweated nearly 2 liters and dropped about 1.5% of their body mass; runners replace only a fraction of their losses. Louise went the other way.

And heat alone doesn't explain who collapses. In one hot half-marathon, 12 of 18 runners topped 40°C (max 41.7°C) with zero heat-illness symptoms. Temperature and collapse don't track together: the number alone doesn't predict who falls. In the lab, heart rate ran about 10 bpm higher at 0.9% dehydration and 18 bpm higher at 2.8% than when euhydrated.

271319
4:304:30FINISH · MARCUS
Marcus

Marcus finishes.

4:30. That lands Marcus in the 17.2% of Boston finishers over 4:30 (median 3:46). The wall arrived on schedule at mile 20 and never left: his second half was 27 minutes slower than his first, the strong positive-split fate of 12.2% of the field. Across 4 million race records, 28% of men and 17% of women show the pacing-defined wall.

415
+24H+24:00THE NEXT DAY
PriyaMarcus

The enzymes peak.

Mean creatine kinase hits ~3,424 IU/L about 24 hours post-race (range 319 to 9,260): "considerable transient exertional rhabdomyolysis." CK-MB reached 130 IU/L, 8.3% of total, levels that would suggest a massive heart attack. Yet scintigraphy showed no myocardial injury. It was all skeletal muscle.

316
The course, mile by mile · illustrative
PRIYA · 3:00MARCUS · 4:30LOUISE · MEDICAL TENT
The wall isn't a time. It's a place. Muscle glycogen runs out around kilometer 30 to 35 no matter your pace: that's 2:08 for a 3-hour marathoner and 3:44 for a 4:30 finisher. Same mile marker. Different o'clock.1

Three runners. None of them is real.

Priya, Marcus, and Louise are illustrative composites built from published data: made-up names and ages, real numbers. Every figure in their arcs is sourced; the people are not.

A

Priya, 34 · the 3:00 qualifier

4:16 / KM · EVEN SPLITS

82% of sub-3:00 Boston runners even-pace their race. The men's wall rate at this level is 1.42%. 4

Illustrative composite · made-up name
B

Marcus, 44 · the 4:30 first-timer

6:24 / KM · FADING LATE

Marcus sits in the strong positive-split cluster (12.2% of the field): second half 27 minutes slower than the first. 4

Illustrative composite · made-up name
C

Louise, 56 · the medical tent

DNF · WEIGHT GAIN

A hyponatremia thread: weight gain during the race was the strongest predictor. Fluid type didn't matter. 2

Illustrative composite · made-up name

Do 43% of runners really hit the wall?

Ask runners and 43% say they've hit the wall. Measure pacing and the figure is 17 to 28%. The definition gap is the story: only 70% of self-reported wall-hitters showed a matching slowdown.

43%Self-reported hitting the wall (Buman et al. 2008, n=31517; original via Smyth 202115). Risk peaked at mile 21. Men, short longest-runs, and expecting the wall raised the odds.
28% / 17%Pacing-defined wall (≥20% late-race slowdown) in 4M+ records: men / women. (Smyth, PLoS One 202115)
17.6% / 9.7%Berlin 1999 to 2025, n=873,334; sub-3:00 men just 1.42%. (Scientific Reports 202612, media-reported)

What if you fueled differently?

Drag the intake slider and watch the guideline band change, and notice what doesn't change: the mechanism. In-race carbohydrate (30 to 90 g/h) spared 25% of type-I fiber glycogen use and stretched time to exhaustion from 104 to 132 minutes.14

60 g/h
Up to 60 g/h: the band for 2 to 3 h effortsJeukendrup guideline bands18
Type-I fibers spared 25%; exhaustion pushed 104 → 132 minTsintzas et al. 199614. The mechanism, whatever your band.

Verdict: covers 2 to 3 hours. The marathon band.

Ceilings, labeled. Glucose-only absorption maxes around 0.8 to 1.0 g/min (intestinal transport limit); glucose + fructose reaches ~1.7 g/min. So 90 g/h only works with multiple transportable carbs. 18

So what did 26.2 miles teach us?

The wall is a place, not a time: kilometers 30 to 35, where the glycogen math (5 mmol per kilogram per kilometer times 42.2 kilometers) finally outruns the tank. Priya's even pacing kept her clear of it; Marcus met it on schedule; and Louise's tent is the twist, because 13% of Boston finishers were hyponatremic and the strongest predictor was weight gain, not dehydration. Three runners, one clock, and every beat of it published somewhere.

How this was built.

Every number in this essay was read from a real published source in October 2026. Superscript numbers point to the notes above, which name each source and say plainly where each figure comes from; the math behind every derivation is shown in the text. The data behind the clock and the charts are published as CSV files in data/twentysix-two/, with a README listing sources, access dates, and transformations. Scope: no marathon-race-specific cardiac drift curve exists; all drift data are lab-based. GI distress, cumulative impact loading, and the post-marathon immune "open window" are outside this essay's scope; nearly all data are recreational/sub-elite.

The Most Expensive Steps

By Jonathan Byrne, DO · October 2026

Why this essay: Energy cost is the hidden tax on every patient I see who walks differently.

FIRST STOP

Below is a room of 1,000 walkers, and each figure glows brighter the more oxygen its owner pays per step. Click any figure to read its fare, or press the button to reveal the most expensive step in the room. As you read on, the fare meter above climbs from 1.0× to 7.7×.

Modeled mix, not a census14151617

Click any figure

Condition, fare per meter, walking speed, and daily steps. Every figure is sourced.

Can you find the most expensive step in this room?

The most expensive step in the room costs 7.7× the cheapest one1, and the people paying the highest fares walk the fewest steps of anyone here.
NEXT STOP

Two ways to bill a walk. Only one is the fare.

There are two ways to bill a walk. O₂ rate (milliliters per kilo per minute) is how hard the engine works. O₂ cost (milliliters per kilo per meter) is the actual fare. People almost always slow down to protect the engine, so cost per meter is the comparison that counts1. Flip the switch and watch what happens to the same walkers when the accounting changes:

The full numbers behind the bars, priced per meter against the intact-walker baseline of ~0.15 mL O₂/kg/m21:

FARE PAID

Fewer steps, roughly double the oxygen.

Two receipts, with the arithmetic shown:
